pedagogy.summary: Year-1 children make the leap from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end and counting them, then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The concept underneath the procedure is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object with no gaps or overlaps, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.
bestPractices: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record the result before any ruler is introduced.
Insist the units are identical in size — deliberately contrast a row measured with mixed-size units so children see why equal units matter.
Make iteration self-checking: units abut with no gaps and no overlaps; have children build their own paper ruler by marking off one repeated unit, tying the ruler back to iteration.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Introduce the centimetre ruler as a tool that simply counts the same iterated units, with the start of the object aligned to the beginning of the ruler.
keyRepresentations: Interlocking / unit cubes laid end to end along an object
Paper-clip chains as a non-standard unit
A child-made paper ruler with a single unit marked off repeatedly
commonMisconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.

learn.summary: Year-1 children move from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end, counting them with no gaps or overlaps, and then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The core concept is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object completely, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.

activities.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
feedback: If there is a gap between cubes, run a finger along the uncovered stretch and ask: is that length being counted? Close the gap and re-count.
If two cubes overlap, point out that the same stretch is being counted twice; separate them so they just abut.
When the row is clean and gap-free, confirm the count and always restate it with the unit: 'about 8 cubes long.'

In a digital version the running counter can redden or refuse to total a gappy or overlapping row, and only count a cleanly tiled row — so the no-gaps/no-overlaps rule is felt, not just told. This live recompute is one optional way to make the rule self-checking.
activities.rationale: Year-1 children often slide units without abutting them exactly and are not concerned about accuracy, so self-checking iteration (abutting units, finger-check, or a recompute that only counts a clean row) targets the actual procedural leap of covering the length rather than merely placing units along it.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.
Run a finger along the pencil to check no uncovered stretch is left between cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

activities.title: Why the units must all be the same size
feedback: If the child counts mixed sizes as one total, pause on the '3 large and 4 small' challenge: are these 7 of the same thing? Establish that the units must all match before the count means anything.
After re-measuring with one size, confirm the total and connect it back to the clean, equal-unit row.
Ask 'would bigger units give you more or fewer?' to check they expect a larger unit to give a smaller count.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting equal versus mixed units exposes the equal-unit rule directly; this addresses the documented misconception of counting mixed-size units as a single total.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Measure the book again, but this time use a bin that has a few oversized blocks mixed in with the small cubes.
Report the total and check whether it makes sense.
Try the challenge: '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks laid in a row — is the book 7 blocks long?' Explain your answer.
Re-measure the book using only one size of unit and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is only meaningful when every unit is the same size; mixing sizes makes the count nonsense.

activities.title: Length is extent, not how many pieces
feedback: If the child says the 6-match row is longer because it has more pieces, lay the two rows side by side aligned at one end so they can see whether the extents match.
When asked 'what are you counting?', steer from 'the matches' toward 'the length' — the number of pieces alone does not tell you the length unless the pieces are the same size.
If the child lines the rows up and finds they reach the same point, confirm they are the same length and ask how aligning at one end let them tell.
activities.rationale: Children often judge length by cardinality, calling a row of more, smaller items 'longer'. The two rows are set up to be the same total length (an off-stage setup condition the child is not told); direct side-by-side comparison re-anchors length as extent independent of the number of pieces.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Look at two rows of matches: one row made of 6 short matches and one row made of 5 longer matches.
Decide which row is longer, or whether they are the same length, and say what you are counting.
Lay the two rows directly side by side, aligned at one end, to check your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Length is how far something extends, not how many pieces make up the row; more pieces does not mean longer.

activities.title: Build a paper ruler and read a centimetre ruler
feedback: If the child lines the object up with '1', show that the stretch from 0 to '1' is already one unit, so reading the numeral at the far end gives one centimetre too many; realign to 0 and re-read.
If they read off the last numeral the object touches without aligning the start, go back to the paper ruler to re-connect numerals to counted units.
Confirm the recorded result always carries its unit ('15 cm'), not a bare number.
In a digital version a virtual ruler can be required to align at 0 before it reads out, linking the tiled units to the tool. This is one optional way to make the zero-start concrete.
activities.rationale: Building a paper ruler from a single repeated unit ties the ruler back to iteration, and keeps ruler work light at this age. Starting at '1' or reading the last numeral touched are common Year-1 errors the zero-alignment work addresses.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and then standard units, and begin to use a ruler.

Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Take a strip of paper and mark off one chosen unit over and over, end to end, to make your own ruler.
Use your paper ruler to measure a short object, counting the units.
Now take a centimetre ruler and line its start (the 0) up with one end of the object, not the '1' mark.
Read off how many centimetres long the object is and record it as a number with its unit, e.g. '15 cm'.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is just a tool that counts the same iterated units; you start from zero because the numerals name the units of space already covered.

activities.title: Spot-the-gap and how-many checks
feedback: For a 'spot the gappy row' choice, name exactly what is wrong with each rejected row — a gap, an overlap, or mixed-size units.
For a how-many answer that is off by one, check where the count started: for a cube row, the first cube is counted as 1; for a ruler picture, the object should start at the 0 mark.
Use these as checks after hands-on practice, not instead of it.
activities.rationale: Recognition items and sliders can check the idea and a spot-the-gap step is discriminating, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the hand-action of building a clean row; keep these as post-practice checks.
learnerActions: Look at several pictured rows and pick which one has been measured correctly (no gaps, no overlaps, equal units).
For a tidy row of cubes, say or set a slider to how many cubes long it is.
For a ruler picture, say how many centimetres long the object is.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise a correctly measured row and read a count, but recognising one does not by itself build the skill of producing a clean row yourself.

constraints: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record before any ruler is introduced.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Keep ruler work light at this age; a child-made paper ruler tying the ruler back to a single repeated unit is the bridge to the centimetre ruler.

Recognition/selection items (spot-the-gap, how-many sliders) check understanding but do not by themselves build the hand-action of iterating and fixing a gappy row; use them as post-practice checks, not the main activity.

A static tap-to-reveal of a cube-row or ruler ('each cube = one length-unit', '0 starts here') can clarify the meaning of the marks as a reference, but a fixed image cannot be re-tiled by the child; pair it with hands-on or interactive iteration.

Physical cubes and an on-screen model offer different experiences; neither is claimed as the only way to learn iteration. Prefer whichever lets the child iterate units and get honest feedback on gaps, overlaps and mixed sizes.
When probing cardinality-vs-length, present or compare rows by aligning the objects side by side at one end; reteaching may require returning to direct length comparison as a prerequisite.

The matches example only demonstrates cardinality-vs-length if the two rows are genuinely the same total length; set the rows to be physically equal but do NOT tell the child they are equal, so the comparison stays open and is discovered by aligning them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D as 'poor' because length is one-dimensional, and dialogue/conversation as 'poor' for a procedural skill. These catalog fit-rankings are not retained as universal pedagogical laws; the relevant objective limit (recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction) is kept, but claims that a static image or a conversation 'cannot teach' are softened or dropped.
The UK National Curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year-1 ruler claim accordingly.

Self-audit of the matches example: a row of 6 shorter matches and a row of 5 longer matches must be set to the same total length to illustrate cardinality-vs-length. This equality is a setup condition kept off-stage; the child-facing prompt no longer states the rows are equal (that would give away the answer) and instead offers 'same length' as one allowed answer the child can reach by aligning the rows.

Self-audit of ruler logic: aligning the object end with 0 (not '1') is correct — the space before the '1' mark is already one unit — so reading from '1' loses a unit; this correction is retained in the activity.

Corrected the cardinality activity on independent review: the prior feedback 'end to end' (which joins rows lengthwise) was already changed to side-by-side alignment, and the learner-facing setup that revealed the rows as 'the same total length' has now been removed so the probe is neither leading nor self-answering; the equality remains only as an off-stage setup condition in the constraints and rationale.

probeDeeper: You said 8 — 8 what? Point to one of them.
If I measured this same book with these bigger blocks instead, would I get more than 8 or fewer than 8? Why?
Watch — I'll lay them like this (place with a gap). Is that measuring properly? What's wrong with it?
Can you start the ruler somewhere other than the end and still get the right length?
assess.correctAnswer: The child lays identical units end to end from one end of the book with no gaps or overlaps, counts the length-units (not the objects at random), states and records the count WITH a unit ('about 12 cubes' / '15 cm'), and — when they reach for the ruler — aligns its start (0) with the end of the book rather than the '1' mark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps or overlaps: lays units with spaces between them or overlapping, as if measuring is 'putting things along' the object rather than covering its whole length with no holes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: have them run a finger along the object to feel the uncovered length between cubes; use abutting, self-checking units and re-count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cubes placed with visible gaps or overlapping; the child still counts them and offers a number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-size units counted as equal: combines cubes and larger blocks and reports one total, not noticing the units differ.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose the '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks — is it 7 blocks long?' challenge; establish that measuring units must all be the same size, then re-measure with one size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A row of different-sized objects counted as a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts discrete objects, not length (cardinality): judges length by how many pieces there are, so a row of more, smaller units is called 'longer' than an equal-length row of fewer, larger units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the matches-experiment discussion and to direct length comparison so length is re-anchored as extent independent of the number of pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown two equal-length rows, the child says the one with more items is longer; answers 'what are you counting?' with 'the cubes' not 'the length'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler read from '1': treats the numerals as signals for where to start counting, so lines the book up with the '1' mark or reports the last numeral touched.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 0 is the start and that a numeral names the units of space already covered; keep ruler work light at this age and build a paper ruler by iterating a single unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Object aligned to the '1' on the ruler, or the final numeral crossed read off as the length; answer off by one.

responseLevels.gap: Lays units with gaps/overlaps or mixes sizes, or gives a bare number with no unit, or judges length by how many pieces there are regardless of the actual extent.
responseLevels.full: Lays identical units with no gaps or overlaps from one end, counts the length-units, records the number with its unit, aligns the ruler's zero, and can say a bigger unit would give a smaller count.
responseLevels.partial: Lays equal units end to end and counts them, but the procedure is fragile: e.g. iterates cubes cleanly yet starts the ruler at '1', or omits the unit unless prompted — succeeds in the practised case but does not transfer to the ruler.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a book, a tub of same-size cubes with a few larger blocks mixed in, and a centimetre ruler. Say: 'Measure how long this book is and tell me the number.' Do not tell them how. Watch how they lay the units, whether they mix sizes, and where they start the ruler; then ask them to write the result down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept produces a clean, gap-free row of equal units and a number-with-unit, and starts the ruler at zero. A child who lacks it reveals precisely which sub-idea is missing in the way they lay and read — gaps/overlaps, mixed units, counting objects, or starting at 1 — none of which a child with the full concept does. The performance is watched, never asked about.
